forces: Mixed chorus and orchestra with organ
performers: Wiener Staatsopernchor; Wiener Philharmoniker; Franz Sauer, organ; Bruno Walter, conductor
recorded: 26 July 1956, Small Festival Hall, Salzburg; live
intro: The Lacrimosa turns two sighing violin bars into a choral ascent that seems to run out of breath. Bruno Walter conducts the Vienna choir and orchestra, recorded live in Salzburg in 1956.

sections.label: A · Sighing strings, rising choir
sections.mNote: Short violin phrases surround the choir’s climb

sections.label: B · Huic ergo, softly
sections.mNote: Repeated choral notes over a wandering bass

sections.label: A′ · The plea for rest
sections.mNote: The opening melody returns with dona eis requiem

sections.label: Coda · Amen in D major
sections.mNote: Two held chords bring the prayer to rest

cues.title: Two bars of sighs
cues.text: Violins and violas begin alone, their short phrases caught between little silences. The choir takes up the lament over the same faltering accompaniment. The metre is 12/8: four slow beats, each divided into three.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Dover reprint, p. 49, bars 1–4: upper strings alone for two bars, then choir and lower instruments. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/79/IMSLP758680-PMLP2751-Mozart_Requiem%2C_K.626_-_Full_Score.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Rising from the ashes
cues.text: At the words about rising from the ashes, the choir itself climbs, step by step. Separated syllables grow into longer notes and the phrase swells to forte. The violins keep catching their breath beneath it.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Dover reprint, p. 50, bars 5–8: qua resurget ex favilla, judicandus homo reus; rising vocal parts, crescendo and forte.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Eight bars in Mozart’s hand
cues.text: In Mozart’s manuscript the Lacrimosa breaks off after eight bars. After his death, Constanze arranges for the unfinished Requiem to be completed. Franz Xaver Süssmayr supplies the rest of this movement in the version performed here.
cues.evidence: Leopold Nowak, Neue Mozart-Ausgabe, Requiem, volume 2, foreword, pp. VII and XIII–XV: the manuscripts and the completion arranged by Constanze. https://dme.mozarteum.at/DME/objs/pdf/nma_14_-23_-3_eng.pdf. The eight-bar fragment is also described by Jan Swafford: https://www.bso.org/works/mozart-requiem

cues.title: Eybler’s two added bars
cues.text: On 21 December 1791 Joseph Eybler signs a declaration that Constanze has entrusted Mozart’s unfinished Requiem to him; he promises to finish it by the middle of Lent. His additions run from the Dies irae to this Lacrimosa, where he writes two soprano bars and stops. The task passes to Süssmayr.
cues.evidence: Leopold Nowak, Neue Mozart-Ausgabe, Requiem, foreword, p. VII (Eybler’s declaration of 21 December 1791 and his traces in the manuscript “from the Dies irae up to the two measures appended to the Lacrimosa”) and p. XV (the two soprano measures; Eybler “shied away” from the new composition); Süssmayr takes over. https://dme.mozarteum.at/DME/objs/pdf/nma_14_-23_-3_eng.pdf

cues.title: The same melody asks
cues.text: The opening melody returns in D minor, now carrying “Dona eis requiem” — grant them rest. The choir sings it forte, with basset horns and bassoons alongside. The violin sighs are still there, between the beats.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Dover reprint, p. 53, bars 20–24: instrumental preparation and return of the opening vocal melody at bar 22, with the new petition.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Amen turns to major
cues.text: The final Amen stretches over two held chords. G minor settles into D major, with F♯ brightening the last chord. The violins finish their little falling figures and come to rest with the voices.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Dover reprint, p. 54, final two bars: G-minor to D-major plagal cadence, with F♯ in the final chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The prayer drops to piano
transitions.how: The choir drops to piano for “Huic ergo”. Basset horns, bassoons, trumpets and timpani rest. The upper voices repeat notes while the choral bass steps down and back up beneath them; little rests still divide the string accompaniment. The prayer works its way back to D minor.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Dover reprint, pp. 51–52, bars 14–19: piano at bar 15, resting winds and brass, and the cadence at Domine.

transitions.title: The violin sighs return
transitions.how: Two instrumental bars bring back the violins’ rising-and-falling figure. The low strings resume their short, separated notes, and the choir returns forte in D minor with “Dona eis requiem”. Basset horns and bassoons reinforce the voices; trumpets and timpani punctuate the phrase.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Dover reprint, p. 53, bars 20–24: the two-bar instrumental link and the choral return at bar 22.

transitions.title: G minor settles into D major
transitions.how: The choir holds a G-minor chord on the first syllable of Amen while the violins finish their falling figures. The bass moves from G to D. An F♯ in the final chord turns the close to D major, and the strings finally sustain their notes with the singers.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Dover reprint, p. 54, bars 29–30: held G-minor and D-major chords, with the moving violin phrase over the first.

source.title: Mozart–Süssmayr Requiem, Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Dover unabridged reprint
source.locator: Printed pp. 49–54: two bars of upper strings, the rising choral lament, the quiet Huic ergo and the final G-minor to D-major Amen. The organ part is discussed in Nowak’s Neue Mozart-Ausgabe foreword, p. XX.

timeline.note: Violins and violas play alone for two bars, their short phrases broken by rests.
The choir enters above the continuing violin sighs, joined by bassoons and low strings.
The choir climbs to forte; trumpets and timpani strike at the top of the phrase.
The choir sings Huic ergo softly over strings and organ; basset horns, bassoons, trumpets and timpani rest.
The opening melody returns with dona eis requiem, reinforced by low reeds above the violin sighs.
The choir holds the two chords of Amen while the violins finish their falling figures; the last chord is D major.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Wiener Staatsopernchor (chorus), Wiener Philharmoniker (orchestra), Franz Sauer (organ), Bruno Walter (conductor)
fields.note: This movement is for chorus, without a solo vocal part; the concert’s vocal solo quartet is not credited as singing here. Commons and Internet Archive name the Wiener Staatsopernchor; the festival catalogue uses Konzertvereinigung Wiener Staatsopernchor. The primary concert archive confirms Walter, the orchestra, all four concert soloists and Franz Sauer, but leaves its choir field blank. Ira Malaniuk, Anton Dermota and Cesare Siepi belong to the full concert cast, not to an invented solo entrance in this movement.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Traditional Süssmayr completion of Mozart’s Lacrimosa; performing edition and Walter’s alterations unidentified.
fields.note: Mozart’s surviving draft breaks off after bar 8. The conventional completion continues the movement and closes with the short Amen, rather than a later reconstructed Amen fugue. The NMA distinguishes Eybler’s separate attempted continuation from Süssmayr’s completed version. The upload does not identify its performing edition; no second-by-second authorship seam or session-specific trombone cut list is claimed.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The primary concert archive identifies Thursday 26 July 1956; Commons, Internet Archive and the discography agree. This is the live performance date, not the date of first publication, a later commercial issue, digitisation or upload.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Small Festival Hall (Kleines Festspielhaus), Salzburg, Austria
fields.note: The Vienna Philharmonic event archive supplies Small Festival Hall. Internet Archive calls the source a live Salzburg Festival performance; the discography uses the broader Festspielhaus designation. No studio session, microphone layout or original recording medium is inferred.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The carrier actually used for this upload is unidentified. The discography lists Cetra, Nuova Era, Seven Seas and Orfeo issues of this performance. The official festival catalogue documents an Orfeo CD in 1996, but neither source ties that issue to the Ogg. A known issue is not a demonstrated transfer source.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: No matrix, take or side identifiers are supplied for the source used. The file is a complete movement from a live performance; neither a shellac carrier nor an original tape generation is established. No physical side join is assigned to a musical event.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: D. Benjamin Miller is the Commons uploader, not an established transfer or mastering engineer. The Internet Archive uploader/scanner fields document repository submission, not who digitised, edited or restored the recording. No transfer-engineer credit has been found.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: Internet Archive added/public date is 4 June 2018; Commons upload is 5 June 2018. These are not transfer dates. The embedded Commons digitizing year 1956 duplicates the performance year without a transfer history and is not accepted as such evidence. The 1996 Orfeo issue is also not assigned as the date of this transfer.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Internet Archive lists the corresponding Ogg Vorbis movement file as an original upload; Commons supplies Ogg Vorbis and an MP3 access derivative.
fields.note: Here original means the repository’s uploaded file, not an original session master. The chain from the unidentified physical or broadcast source to the Ogg is undocumented. Session medium, tape generation, speed correction, equalisation, noise reduction, editing and restoration settings remain unknown; no such processing is inferred from the transfer’s sound.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying Mozart–Süssmayr composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Mozart died in 1791 and Süssmayr in 1803; the traditional full score was published in 1800. This is a term-based assessment of the historical composition, not a worldwide clearance, a licence for a modern critical edition, or evidence about the sound recording.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 1 — territorial recording claim: Commons applies PD-EU-audio; upstream Internet Archive applies Public Domain Mark 1.0.
fields.note: The documented fact is the sources’ sound-recording rights assertion. PD-EU-audio is territorial: US status is not established, and no worldwide clearance is claimed. Public Domain Mark is not CC0 or a performer’s licence. The 1956 performance date does not prove first lawful publication or communication before 1963; that history is unestablished. The known 1996 Orfeo issue and 2018 uploads are not substituted for it. Admission therefore uses the explicit Commons PD-EU-audio route, not a calculated pre-1963-publication claim.

composer.background:
When Leopold Mozart arrived in Vienna on 11 February 1785, the copyist was still writing out his son’s new concerto for that evening’s concert at the Mehlgrube. Wolfgang had been so busy supervising the copying that he had found no time to try the finale through. This was K. 466 in D minor: restless, syncopated strings, then a piano entering with a tune of its own. Leopold thought the concert splendid.

The next day, Haydn heard three quartets at Wolfgang’s home. Leopold recorded his verdict in a letter to Nannerl begun on 14 February: “Before God, and as an honest man, I tell you that your son is the greatest composer I know, personally or by name.” Haydn praised his taste and his knowledge of composition. Mozart would dedicate the quartets to him.
